prompt: What is a security group attached to?
hint: It is why two machines in one subnet can have different rules.

choices.text: A subnet, like a route table
choices.why: That is the network ACL. A security group judges each interface on its own, even between neighbours.

choices.text: A network interface
choices.why: Right. The interface a machine, a load balancer or a database talks through.

choices.text: The VPC as a whole, at its edge
choices.why: A group belongs to a VPC but filters nothing until an interface carries it.

choices.text: The internet gateway, for traffic from outside
choices.why: A gateway forwards and translates; it carries no group. Traffic between two machines inside never meets it.

prompt: `db-sg` has no outbound rule at all. Can the database still answer the application's queries?
hint: What does stateful mean for a reply?

choices.text: No: a packet that leaves needs an outbound rule
choices.why: That is how a network ACL behaves. A security group remembers the connections it let in.

choices.text: Yes: the group is stateful, and replies leave
choices.why: Right. The group is stateful. What the empty outbound list stops is the database opening a connection of its own.

choices.text: Just when the default group is attached as well
choices.why: A second group would add rules, but none is needed for replies; the first group already lets them out.

choices.text: Within its own subnet alone
choices.why: Subnets play no part in a security group's decision, and the application sits in another subnet anyway.

prompt: Why does `app-sg` let in port 8080 from `alb-sg` rather than from `10.20.0.0/20`, the range of `public-a`?
hint: What else has an address in `public-a`?

choices.text: A rule cannot name an address range inside the VPC
choices.why: It can; the load balancer's own rule names a range. The question is what the range would let in.

choices.text: References are checked faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason, and the lesson makes no claim about it.

choices.text: The range would also admit the NAT gateway
choices.why: Right. A reference means the load balancer whatever its addresses; a range means whatever happens to sit in it.

choices.text: The load balancer has no address of its own in `public-a`
choices.why: It has interfaces in the public subnets; the trouble is that it is not the only thing there.

prompt: The shop wants everybody to reach the load balancer on 443 except `198.51.100.7`. Which change does it?
hint: One of the two filters has no way to say no.

choices.text: A deny rule for that address in `alb-sg`, written before the allow
choices.why: A security group holds only allows, and its rules are not ordered; there is no deny to write.

choices.text: An inbound deny in the public subnets' network ACL, numbered below the allow for 443
choices.why: Right. That is rule 90 in the shop's `public` network ACL; the packet is dropped before `alb-sg` sees it.

choices.text: An outbound deny for that address in `alb-sg`, so that no reply reaches it
choices.why: Outbound rules are allows too, and replies leave by themselves because the group is stateful.

choices.text: Remove `0.0.0.0/0` from `alb-sg` and add the customers' addresses one by one
choices.why: Nobody knows the customers' addresses in advance, and a group holds 60 inbound rules by default.

prompt: moto's default security group had no inbound rule. What does AWS's default security group allow in?
hint: Machines left on the default can talk to each other.

choices.text: Nothing, as in moto
choices.why: AWS's default has one inbound rule that moto leaves out.

choices.text: SSH from anywhere, so that a first machine can be reached
choices.why: No default rule opens a port to the internet; an SSH rule from anywhere is something people add, and regret.

choices.text: All traffic from interfaces that carry the same group
choices.why: Right. A rule whose source is the group itself, so members reach each other and nothing else reaches them.

choices.text: All traffic from inside the VPC's range
choices.why: The rule names the group, not the range: a machine elsewhere in the VPC without the default group is not let in.

prompt: `create-security-group` has just made `db-sg`. Which of these hold for it before any rule is added? Choose all that apply.
hint: The transcript printed its one rule.

choices.text: It lets nothing in
choices.why: Right. A new group has no inbound rule.

choices.text: It lets every outbound connection out
choices.why: Right. `True -1 0.0.0.0/0`: outbound, every protocol, everywhere.
A security group denies nothing by name; that deny lives in the network ACL.

choices.text: It filters the subnets of the data tier
choices.why: It filters the interfaces that carry it, wherever they are, and none carries it yet.

choices.text: It can hold only allow rules
choices.why: Right. That is true of every security group.

prompt: In what order does a network ACL read its rules?
hint: The numbers are the order.

choices.text: All together, and a deny anywhere wins
choices.why: That is closer to how IAM judges a policy. A network ACL stops at the first rule that matches.

choices.text: By number, lowest first; the first match decides
choices.why: Right. Which is why the shop's deny is rule 90 and the allow for 443 is rule 100.

choices.text: In the order the rules were created
choices.why: Creation order plays no part; the number does. Steps of ten leave room to insert one between two others.

choices.text: By number, highest first, so the `*` rule comes first
choices.why: The `*` rule, 32767, is the last word: it denies only what nothing else matched.

prompt: A network ACL's inbound rules are: 100 allows TCP 443 from `0.0.0.0/0`; 200 denies everything from `198.51.100.7/32`. Does `198.51.100.7` get through on port 443?
hint: Read the rules the way the network ACL does.

choices.text: Yes: rule 100 matches first and allows it
choices.why: Right. The deny is never reached for that packet. Numbering it below 100, as the shop's rule 90 is, is what makes it work.

choices.text: No: a deny beats an allow wherever it sits
choices.why: That is the rule for IAM policies, not for network ACLs, where the first match decides.

choices.text: No: the more specific rule, the `/32`, wins
choices.why: Longest prefix decides routes. A network ACL goes by rule number, whatever the prefixes.

choices.text: It depends on the security group, which decides between the two
choices.why: The network ACL decides on its own, before the security group sees the packet.

prompt: Why does the `public` network ACL allow outbound TCP 1024 to 65535 to everywhere?
hint: Where does the reply to a customer go?

choices.text: So that the load balancer can open connections to any server
choices.why: Servers listen on low, well-known ports such as 443. High ports are where clients wait for replies.

choices.text: Replies go to the client's ephemeral port
choices.why: Right. The reply is a new packet to the network ACL, so it needs its own rule; AWS recommends the whole range from 1024.

choices.text: Because AWS adds that rule to every network ACL it creates
choices.why: A new network ACL has only the `*` rules. The shop wrote this one.

choices.text: To let the security groups do their part
choices.why: The security groups do not depend on it; the replies they let out would die at this edge without it.

prompt: `describe-network-acls` numbers the last rule of every network ACL, the one the console shows as `*`, as rule ___.
hint: The transcript of the default network ACL printed it twice.

prompt: A network ACL remembers nothing about a connection, so a reply needs a rule of its own: the word for that property is ___.
hint: The opposite of a security group's.

prompt: moto answered `[]` for the entries of a network ACL it had just created. What does a new custom network ACL let through on AWS?
hint: Compare it with the default network ACL.

choices.text: Everything, like the default network ACL
choices.why: The default allows everything because of its rule 100. A new one has no such rule.

choices.text: Nothing until rules are added: it has only the `*` denies
choices.why: Right. Which is why associating an empty new network ACL with a subnet cuts it off at once.

choices.text: Inbound nothing, outbound everything, like a new security group
choices.why: That is a new security group. A network ACL's two `*` rules deny in both directions.

choices.text: Whatever the subnet's security groups allow
choices.why: The two filters are independent, and subnets do not have security groups; interfaces do.

prompt: A customer's packet reaches the load balancer, and the load balancer replies. Put the checks in the order they happen.
hint: In, the subnet comes before the interface; out, the other way round.
items: `alb-sg` lets the reply out, since it belongs to an allowed connection
trap: The reply meets the security group before the network ACL, because the interface is inside the subnet.

prompt: In the third walk the load balancer sends straight to the database on 5432. Which filter refuses it?
hint: Every address check allowed it.

choices.text: The `public` network ACL, on the way out
choices.why: Rule 120 outbound allows everything to `10.20.0.0/16`.

choices.text: `data-a`'s network ACL, on the way in
choices.why: `data-a` is on the default network ACL, which lets everything in.

choices.text: `db-sg`, which trusts only interfaces carrying `app-sg`
choices.why: Right. The load balancer carries `alb-sg`. The refusal is by identity, which no address rule could make.

choices.text: `alb-sg`, which has no rule for 5432
choices.why: `alb-sg`'s outbound rule allows everything; the refusal happens at the database's interface.

prompt: Before changing a rule, the shop wants AWS to say whether the load balancer could reach the database, and which rule would stop it, without sending traffic. Which tool is that?
hint: One tool records what happened; the other reads the configuration.

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs
choices.why: Flow Logs record connections that were attempted. With no traffic there is nothing for them to record.

choices.text: VPC Reachability Analyzer
choices.why: Right. It reads route tables, network ACLs and security groups between two points and names the blocking rule. Ten cents an analysis in São Paulo.

choices.text: `describe-security-group-rules`
choices.why: It lists rules; it does not combine them with routes and network ACLs into an answer about a path.

choices.text: moto, since it stores every rule
choices.why: moto stores the rules and filters nothing, so it cannot say whether a packet would pass.

prompt: At the price the lesson read for São Paulo, how many dollars do five Reachability Analyzer analyses cost?
hint: One line of the VPC offer.

prompt: Somebody moves the data subnets onto a new network ACL with one inbound rule, 100 allowing TCP 5432 from `10.20.0.0/16`, and no outbound rule of its own. The application's queries stop working. Why?
hint: The queries get in. What about the answers?

choices.text: `db-sg` refuses the queries, since the network ACL changed
choices.why: The two filters are independent; `db-sg` still trusts `app-sg` exactly as before.

choices.text: The inbound rule is wrong: 5432 must be allowed from `app-sg`
choices.why: A network ACL cannot name a security group; an address range is what it takes, and this one is right.

choices.text: The replies leave for the application's ephemeral ports, and the `*` rule denies them
choices.why: Right. A network ACL is stateless: without an outbound rule for 1024 to 65535 towards the VPC, every reply dies at the edge of the data subnets.

choices.text: A subnet cannot leave the default network ACL while machines run in it
choices.why: Replacing the association works at any time, which is exactly how this outage could happen at once.

prompt: Match each description to what it describes.
hint: Two filters and two tools.

pairs.left: numbered allow and deny rules at a subnet's edge
allow rules on an interface that can name another group
a record per interface of each connection, with `ACCEPT` or `REJECT`
an answer about a path, read from the configuration

prompt: An engineer tidies the `public` network ACL and deletes inbound rule 110, TCP 1024 to 65535 from anywhere. Customers still reach the shop. What stops working?
hint: Which connections in the public subnets are opened from the inside?

choices.text: Nothing, since replies to customers leave under the outbound rules
choices.why: That covers the connections customers open. The NAT gateways open connections too, and their replies come in.

choices.text: The application's calls out through NAT
choices.why: Right. The NAT gateways sit in the public subnets; the payment provider's answers come back to ephemeral ports, which only rule 110 let in.

choices.text: Customers on IPv6
choices.why: The rules in question are IPv4, and the shop's customers reach it over IPv4.

choices.text: The deny for `198.51.100.7`, which depended on rule 110
choices.why: Rule 90 stands on its own: it is read first and matches that address whatever comes after.

prompt: Which of these did the lab show about moto? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three are about what it stores or refuses; two are about what it would have to carry.

choices.text: It refuses the same security group rule added twice
choices.why: Right. `InvalidPermission.Duplicate`, as on AWS.

choices.text: It dropped the packets from `198.51.100.7`
choices.why: No packet existed to drop; the walk was reasoning from the rules.

choices.text: Its default security group has no inbound rule
choices.why: Right. AWS's has the rule that trusts the group itself.

choices.text: A new network ACL in it starts with no rules at all
choices.why: Right. AWS's starts with the two `*` denies.

choices.text: It wrote a Flow Log of the load balancer's refused request
choices.why: There was no request and no Flow Log; both belong to AWS, and neither was run.
